author: Mzi Velapi
title: Memorial service held for victims of the Strand mass shooting
content:
In the early hours of Sunday morning, 27 September, gunmen opened fire on patrons at a shisanyama in Lwandle, near Cape Town, killing ten people. “Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities. Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained. Lwandle police have opened murder and attempted murder cases,” said the police. The community believes the mass shooting is related to the extortion racket that is ravaging Cape Town townships.


One of the victims, Khululekani Ndlovu, will be laid to rest this weekend. The nine other people killed will be buried next weekend in the Eastern Cape. The Nomzamo Community Hall in Strand, south east of Cape Town, was packed with mourners and members of political parties for the memorial service.


Speaking to

Elitsha

, the chairperson of the police board in South Africa, Francina Lukas, said that extortion and business rivalry and lack of opportunities for young people are some of the factors contributing to high crime rates in the townships of Cape Town. She said that the lack of trust the community has in the police contributes to high crime rate.


“The police need to do much more than what they are doing in terms of compliance to make sure that businesses in the township comply with their licenses and bylaws. But the issue of trust is still a burning issue in our communities. So we need to overcome that issue to see that trust in the police is restored,” she said.


Families of the Strand 10


Speaking on behalf of the Sikweza family who lost their daughter, Avuyile, her uncle, Luyanda Macokeni, said she had plans to return to school next year. The 20-year-old passed her matric in 2024. She applied to continue her education next year and had just received responses from two universities offering her a place to study. She was expected to make a choice between the two. “Avuyile is supposed to the one burying us as elders but we are the ones burying her. It’s not God’s will that we are here today, it is because of someone’s will,” he said.


Siyathemba Jilaji was one of the victims who died on his way to the hospital, according to his friend. “He said he was going to change in the car so when the shooting began, I thought he was still in the car. A bullet grazed me under my arm. After the shooting, I went to the car to check for him. But, I didn’t know that he was amongst the bodies that were lying next to the entrance that I ran past,” she said.


Sivenathi Manxiwa’s father, Lubabalo Ndamane, said that he is not going to forgive the person who murdered his son. “I also don’t want to know who they are. Even if they can be arrested, I would not go to court. I leave everything to God and God will deal with him. I want to know what drove him to shoot at the young people who were out enjoying themselves,” he said.


The 10 people who died during the mass shooting in Strand last weekend

.

Photo from Facebook

.


The police said that the investigation into the mass murder is still ongoing.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Beyond Translation: Reimagining Feminist Funding for Portuguese-Speaking Africa
content:
“Portuguese-speaking Africa is not on the margins of Africa’s feminist movement. It is an essential part of it.”


Across Africa, feminist movements have long challenged systems of inequality, responded to crises, created new possibilities for minoritized and excluded communities. Philanthropy has been integral to advances toward just and equal African societies. Yet within the current global and continental landscape of feminist philanthropy, some communities and movements remain largely unseen. 


The Portuguese-speaking African countries that include Angola, Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Equatorial Guinea and São Tomé and Principe, represent diverse histories, political realities and social contexts. Their feminist movements are dynamic, innovative and deeply rooted in their communities. They are advancing gender justice in contexts shaped by economic deprivation and inequality, climate change, difficult democratic transitions, shrinking civic space and gender-based violence.


Despite this important work, these movements continue to face significant barriers to accessing resources, networks and spaces where Africa’s feminist priorities are shaped. The challenge is not a lack of organizing. It is a fragmented funding ecosystem that has not yet fully recognized or responded to the diversity of Africa’s feminist movements. 


The cost of being overlooked


“This is not simply a language issue. It is a question of equity, power, and whose movements are seen as worthy of sustained investment.”


Language is often treated as a technical issue within philanthropy. But colonial imagined and erected linguistic borders, in reality, determine who participates, whose knowledge is shared, and which movements can access opportunities. Many continental funding opportunities, convenings, research publications and learning spaces are designed primarily in English or, to a lesser extent, French. Organizations from Portuguese-speaking countries frequently face additional costs related to translation, interpretation and participation — costs that are rarely built into funding models.


The result is a structural barrier: organizations with valuable expertise and strong community connections may remain disconnected from funding opportunities, regional conversations and shared learnings, not because of limited impact but because systems were not designed with their inclusion in mind. For philanthropy, this raises a fundamental question: 

What does meaningful inclusion look like when funding systems themselves create barriers to participation?


 


Listening before investing


At the African Women’s Development Fund (AWDF), we recognized that addressing this gap required more than acknowledging the challenge. It required listening, evidence and a deeper understanding of how feminist movements in Portuguese-speaking Africa organize, sustain themselves and envision their futures.


AWDF undertook a

mapping of feminist movements and funding landscapes

 across Portuguese-speaking Africa to better understand not only the barriers facing these movements, but also the opportunities for philanthropy to engage differently. We asked:

What does feminist organizing and funding actually look like across Portuguese-speaking Africa, and what would it take to strengthen these movements for the long term?


The findings provide an important reminder that communities and movements that have historically been overlooked are not waiting to be built. They are already organizing, innovating and creating solutions. What is needed is a funding ecosystem that recognizes their leadership and invests accordingly.


Feminist movements creating new pathways for change


Across the region, feminist organisations are demonstrating resilience, creativity, and strategic vision. There is growing interest in stronger Portuguese-speaking feminist networks that can support collective advocacy, shared learning, and cross-border solidarity. Storytelling and creative expression are being used as powerful organising tools, particularly among younger activists and in rural communities, allowing feminist narratives to emerge from local experiences and knowledge.  For example, our research shows that in São Tomé and Príncipe, informal associations are playing a vital role in mobilising communities through door-to-door outreach and storytelling, while in Equatorial Guinea, feminist collectives are using storytelling, dance, and performance as vehicles for feminist …

author: Awonusi Ayomide Jesudamilare
title: The Grid Inside the Grid
content:
In March, when

Cassava Technologies announced the launch of an AI factory powered by NVIDIA

 in South Africa, the company described it as a turning point. African businesses would gain local access to high-performance computing. Data would remain within African borders. Developers would be able to build models for local languages and local problems.


The promise matters. African researchers and firms cannot participate meaningfully in artificial intelligence if they must rent every unit of computing power from servers abroad. But the most consequential infrastructure inside an AI factory may not be the graphics processor. It may be the electricity connection.


Artificial intelligence is exceptionally energy hungry. The

International Energy Agency expects global electricity consumption by data centers to nearly double by 2030

. The pressure is not evenly distributed. Data centers cluster in particular cities and industrial corridors, where their demand can collide with already constrained transmission systems.


South Africa shows how this collision is being managed. Data center operators are increasingly securing electricity through private renewable plants and wheeling arrangements, which allow power generated in one province to travel across the national network to a customer elsewhere. Teraco, a major operator, is developing a 120-megawatt solar plant in the Free State to supply its facilities in Johannesburg and Cape Town.

Other operators have signed similar agreements

.


This can look like responsible investment. Private procurement adds renewable generation, reduces dependence on coal, and helps large customers avoid drawing all their electricity from local distribution networks.

South Africa’s electricity supply has also improved

 after years of blackouts. Yet the country still needs to

expand and strengthen its transmission network

. A private solar farm does not create a private route from the sun to a server. It still depends on substations, power lines, and grid capacity financed and governed as part of the national system.


The concern is not abstract. In May, community organizations

challenged plans for two Equinix data centers in Cape Town

, arguing that the applications did not provide enough information about electricity demand, water use, emissions, and backup power. The proposed facilities could require up to 160 megawatts combined. The dispute asks a basic democratic question: How should cities weigh private digital investment against competing claims on shared resources?


This is the grid inside the grid: a layer of firm, privately secured electricity built for facilities that cannot tolerate interruption, operating within a public system still struggling to expand transmission and connect new generation. The AI factory may be geographically located in South Africa, but its relationship to the surrounding economy can resemble an enclave. It receives dedicated power, imported equipment, sophisticated cooling, and backup generation. The wider public is promised future innovation, jobs, and growth.


The same tension is visible in Kenya. A proposed $1 billion data center involving Microsoft and the Emirati company G42 was presented as a geothermal-powered foundation for East Africa’s cloud and AI economy. By May 2026,

negotiations had stalled over requests for guaranteed capacity payments

, while the scale of the project’s power requirements remained under discussion. The episode revealed what investment announcements often conceal: Governments may be asked not only to host digital infrastructure but also to guarantee its market and reorganize scarce energy capacity around it.


None of this means African governments should reject data centers. Local computing capacity can reduce latency, support universities and startups, keep sensitive data closer to home, and create alternatives to total dependence on overseas cloud regions. The issue is not whether AI infrastructure should be built. It is whether public systems become stronger because it is built.


That requires more than celebratory language about sovereignty. Governments should disclose the electricity, water, land, tax, and guarantee arrangements attached to large data center projects. New power procurement should demonstrate that it adds generation rather than simply reserving existing transmission capacity. Contracts should require investment in shared grid infrastructure, meaningful local access to computing resources …

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: WoMin
title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.


There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.


Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.


Education is a political commitment


In the 1971 BBC film “

Behind the lines

”, Maria, a Mozambican guerrilla fighter explains that education was at the heart of why she decided to join the liberation struggle. In her experience

“If a girl reached a certain class [The colonialists] said that is enough for us, Africans.”


(Literacy Campaign, Guerrilla warfare in Angola, 1968. Photo: Augusta Conchiglia)


Our feminist

herstories

 across Africa and beyond have been deeply shaped by anti-colonial struggles. It was within the liberation movements that many women and men encountered education as a practice of freedom, in learning to question colonial power, reclaiming their histories and wisdom, fighting to protect their sovereignty and imagining forms of collective life beyond the impositions of heteropatriarchal, capitalist, colonial systems.


As feminist ancestor Nawal El Saadawi reminds us

“good education means creating dissatisfaction and disobedience.”

 Her wordsspeak to the transformative power of education to nurture the critical consciousness needed to both understand the conditions that constrain us and to connect them to our personal experiences, which is fundamental to organise collectively towards liberation.


But liberation cannot be achieved by a few, full liberation requires all of us. Our political project must be sustained by an intentional educational project that deepens our proposals and equips us to build the worlds we envision.


The educator is a pollinator


Through processes of learning, unlearning, relearning and imagining together, we become both teachers and students in our movements. This is one of the many ways in which decolonial feminist popular education inspires us to cultivate relational ways of working together that are grounded in mutual learning, listening, solidarity and care.


Instead of positioning the educator as the one who holds all the answers, popular educators create spaces where all can collectively formulate the questions that emerge from our struggles and where all can develop the knowledge needed to respond.


“Vou aprender a ler

 /

Para ensinar minhas camaradas

 /

I will learn how to read

 /

To teach my comrades”


Brazilian struggle song


The same way bees are essential for healthy environments, popular educators are an important part of feminist movements infrastructure. Popular educators nurture the power that already exists within movements.


Like the flower, each individual carries something that can nourish the collective. Learning is never only for ourselves. What we learn becomes a good we carry around our movements, to share, to exchange, to teach and to transform. Knowledge moves between us, allowing new ideas, possibilities and material actions to be activated. It is through this circulation of knowledge that we can produce the sweet taste of hope needed to build different futures.


Organising and liberating as we educate


“The beast is too big, and we need a political project that inspires us to build something every day and not just to fight and destroy the world as we know it.” –


Sandra, Guatemala


A decolonial feminist popular education praxis can build bridges across our different struggles, experiences, beliefs and movements, creating the conditions to move beyond simply resisting what exists …

author: Mada Masr
title: Matsda2sh journalists forced to read false ‘confessions’ statements to camera, subjected to torture in custody
content:
Several of the Matsda2sh journalists arrested last week were forced to record false “confessions” and subjected to torture and ill-treatment while being held at National Security Agency premises, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are representing the six journalists,

stated

 on Monday morning.


EIPR lawyers attended investigation sessions with five of the independent fact-checking platform’s journalists on Sunday evening, when they were presented before prosecuting authorities for the first time since the start of the security campaign that saw six of Matsda2sh’s journalists arrested and forcibly disappeared within the span of 24 hours between September 28 and 29.


The Supreme State Security Prosecution interrogated Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emaira for over 10 hours beginning on Saturday evening and issued orders he be

held

 in remand for 15 days pending further investigations.


The other five journalists were presented before prosecutors on Sunday evening and were each questioned for over 10 hours over the course of the night.


Lawyers were present with them during the investigation sessions, but the detainees were not allowed to consult with them privately. The prosecution is yet to issue detention orders for Abdallah Qadry, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal.


Lawyers anticipated they would be brought again before prosecutors for further questioning on Monday, with EIPR confirming that they were returned to custody in a location that is unknown to their families and lawyers.


At the time of writing, lawyers representing the journalists were waiting at the security prosecution headquarters but had not yet been allowed to enter the building, as the journalists were not yet present, three of the lawyers who were in attendance during Sunday night’s sessions told Mada Masr.


Lawyers substantiated the journalists’ accounts of torture and ill-treatment during the investigation sessions as well as the fact that officers in charge of their detention and custody across three governorates forced them to read fabricated “confessions” in front of cameras, according to EIPR.


After establishing these accounts of torture and coerced testimony, the lawyers requested that the prosecution look into these accounts as formal victim complaints from the journalists, also demanding that any “confessions” attributed to them during their time in custody be rendered invalid and that the responsible National Security Agency officers be questioned, EIPR stated.


EIPR described the forced confessions as appearing to be “an effort to manufacture evidence that could later be used to convict them.”


Several of the five journalists have asked to be referred for forensic examination to establish a record of the injuries they sustained at the hands of the National Security Agency officers — a request which the prosecution granted on Monday to only one of the journalists, EIPR stated, without specifying whom.


The statement specified that, according to the lawyers, the accusations levied against the journalists were based on an investigation report prepared by a National Security Agency officer maintaining that the journalists launched a social media page “to stir up the Egyptian street and create a revolutionary climate by using technical methods on social media and recruiting people with no political affiliations for their own purposes.”


The three lawyers who were in attendance told Mada Masr that Sunday night’s questioning was general in nature, including questions around their journalistic work methods, how they contacted sources and the nature of those sources. The journalists were also each asked about the nature of their relationships with Matsda2sh and its founder, Abdel Rahman Mansour.


EIPR did not clarify in its statement the charges the journalists were questioned about. However, defense lawyer Nabih al-Genady, who was present at the prosecution headquarters on Monday morning,

said

 that they have been questioned so far in relation to joining a terrorist group, intentionally publishing false news, using social media accounts to circulate ideas calling for the perpetration of terrorist acts, as well as committing a terrorism financing crime.


The prosecution is yet to register its charges as part of an official investigation against the five journalists who were brought in last night.

author: Kévin Drif
title: The North African family French critics couldn’t see
content:
Since her 2016 debut feature

Raw

, the French auteur Julia Ducournau’s films have been a staple of the body horror genre. Her movies reflect an unapologetic approach to exploring physical transformation and the “monstrous feminine,” an idea coined by feminist film scholar Barbara Creed to underscore the significance of gender and sexuality in the construction of monstrosity. In Ducournau’s films, female characters strive for emancipation from social and familial norms through cannibalism or transhumanism. Yet while

Raw

 and her sophomore feature

Titane

 (2021) center white protagonists,

Alpha

 (2025), her third film, foregrounds the complex dynamic of a family of North African descent, marking a significant departure for the auteur. Curiously, this demographic difference has been almost entirely absent from discussions of the film.

Set between the 1980s and 1990s,

Alpha

 follows its 13-year-old eponymous character; her mother, who is a doctor; and her uncle Amin as they confront a mysterious virus that transforms bodies into blue-veined marmoreal statues that eventually turn to dust. Critics have understandably focused on the epidemic narrative, the stigma attached to the infected, and its evocation of the AIDS crisis, but in doing so, they have overlooked another dimension of the story:

Alpha

 is one of the few contemporary French films to place a family of North African origin at the center of a national trauma.

Ducournau hardly conceals the central family’s roots. She casts actors of Algerian, Moroccan, and Iranian descent and the characters move between French and dialectal Arabic. In one scene that features the most cinematic French postcolonial locality — the

banlieue

 —

Alpha

 joins her extended family to share a couscous meal for an Eid celebration. The problem here is not simply that reviewers omitted demographic details but that their silence in effect reproduces a broader tendency and difficulty within French cultural discourse to see race, acknowledge colonial history, and address postcolonial belonging even when it permeates the screen.

Approaching

Alpha

 through a postcolonial lens opens more interpretative possibilities. Consider the body itself, a central concern of Ducournau’s cinema:

Alpha

’s makeshift tattoo, which symbolically binds her to Amin, evokes traditions of Amazigh inking while also drawing attention to the postcolonial body as a site of inscription, memory, and belonging. The gesture turns the body into a site where cultural memory can persist without being explicitly articulated;

Alpha

’s body becomes a postcolonial archive — a place where histories and affiliations that remain largely unspoken can nonetheless be inscribed, carried, and transmitted. Furthermore, the film’s concern with body regulation recalls the colonial politics of visibility explored by Frantz Fanon in his writings on French Algeria, where the control of bodies, especially female bodies through the practice of unveiling, functioned as a mechanism of domination.

Alpha

’s epidemic narrative also takes on new meanings when viewed through the history of North African migration. The AIDS crisis in France disproportionally affected marginalized communities. According to

a 1999 study

 led by the French Institut de veille sanitaire, or Institute of Health Surveillance, between 1978 and 1998, immigrant populations accounted for 14 percent of AIDS cases in France, when they only represented 6 percent of the adult population at the time. Drug users of North African origin infected through contaminated needles, much like Amin, represented the main mode of contamination for heterosexual men and accounted for 45 percent of North African immigrant cases. Still, they remain largely absent from narratives of the epidemic. This omission and silence of the infected is the result of the religious taboo attached to the disease and the larger structural disinterest in these populations. Ducournau’s attention to Amin gestures towards histories that have largely escaped commemoration.

Alpha

’s imagery of suffocation, disease, and social abandonment invites reflection of the lives and afterlives of colonial violence beyond France. The calcification of infected bodies recalls forms of historical petrification through which colonial atrocities are rendered distant, abstract, and invisible within French national memory. The structural and social segregation imposed on the sick in the film, illustrated in the …

author: Saif Eddine Ghobr
title: Capacity Substitution: How Tunisia’s Problems Became Someone Else’s Priorities
content:
In the summer of 2023, a young man from Gafsa tried to cross the Mediterranean on a small boat. He did not make it. His story is one of thousands — and it is increasingly understood by Tunisian institutions through the language of border management. It is also a story about who defines what a problem is.


In June 2023, the European Commission announced a package for Tunisia: up to

€900 million in proposed macro-financial assistance

,

€150 million in budget support

, and

€100 million for border management, search and rescue, anti-smuggling, and returns

. In July, the EU and Tunisia signed a

Memorandum of Understanding

 formalising the partnership. By September, a further

€105 million was allocated

 to migration-related programmes. By December, the €150 million budget-support programme was operational.


The sequence is documented. What it produces institutionally is less visible. This article examines a mechanism I call

capacity substitution

. Capacity building strengthens a state’s ability to solve its own problems. Capacity substitution makes a state more efficient at solving problems defined by someone else. The distinction is simple. Its consequences are not.


Consider Tunisia’s migration apparatus. The EU–Tunisia Memorandum links European support to border management, anti-smuggling operations, search and rescue, and returns. These are legitimate European objectives. They are also objectives that European institutions can define, fund, monitor, and measure. European support has equipped units, funded training, and strengthened interception capacity.


What it has not done — and was not designed to do — is strengthen Tunisia’s capacity to address the economic conditions that generate migration.

Youth unemployment stood at 35.4 percent in 2026

.

Graduate unemployment was 26.6 percent

. Regional inequality remains entrenched.


The argument is not that European funding caused these figures. It is that external funding concentrates institutional development on a specific set of functions. Those functions become better equipped, better staffed, and more internationally connected. The functions that would address the structural conditions producing migration are not developed through an equivalent institutional investment.  This is what capacity substitution describes.


A young unemployed person in Gafsa is unlikely to attempt to cross the Mediterranean simply because Tunisia lacks another surveillance system. The deeper driver is the narrowing of his economic and social horizon. If institutional capacity is concentrated on managing his departure, while the capacities that would address the conditions producing it are not developed through an equivalent investment, then the state becomes more effective at managing the symptom. It remains structurally less equipped to govern the cause. It does not require coercion. It does not require a conspiracy. It only requires that the external priority be better resourced than the domestic one.


Migration is not the only domain where this mechanism operates. European energy cooperation with Tunisia is another. EU funding for renewable energy, electricity interconnection, and green hydrogen is increasingly organised around projects that also serve European energy security: cross-Mediterranean interconnection such as the

ELMED project

, export capacity, and the

decarbonisation of European supply chains.


Domestic energy challenges  subsidy reform, grid reliability, and energy poverty are not absent from the relationship. But they are not the organising priority around which much of the external financing is structured. The result is a similar pattern: institutional capacity is strengthened in functions that serve externally defined priorities, while capacities addressing domestic structural conditions do not necessarily receive an equivalent institutional investment.


What migration and energy share is not a conspiracy. It is a logic. External resources tend to come attached to externally legible priorities. And externally legible priorities tend to be those that serve external needs.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Israel Bans Polanski After UK’s Green Party Votes to Classify Zionism as Racism
content:
The Green Party motion also calls for a single state in historic Palestine with equal rights for all.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

On Sunday, the United Kingdom’s Green Party passed a motion defining Zionism as a form of racism. Within hours of the vote, Israel’s foreign ministry responded, slamming the motion and barring Green Party leader Zack Polanski from entering Israel.

“The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” Israel’s foreign ministry posted on X, speciously comparing the left-wing British political party to the Palestinian resistance group.

The foreign ministry also called on the U.K.’s Labour Party to denounce the motion.

The motion passed at the Green Party’s annual conference on Sunday in a vote of 1,022 to 813. In addition to denouncing Zionism, it calls for a single state in historic Palestine with equal rights for all, with the right of return for Palestinians. The motion also acknowledges the right of Palestinians to resist, and reasserts the Green Party’s commitment to the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) campaign and a total arms embargo.

Israeli politicians from various political parties smeared the motion.

“Those who claim the antisemitic lie that ‘Zionism is racism’ deliberately endanger Jews and Israelis everywhere,” Israeli President Isaac Herzog posted on X after its passage.

Opposition leader Yair Lapid wrote on social media that “the UK Green Party has chosen to side with terrorists and antisemites” as Israel prepares to mark three years since the October 7 attack.

Notably, the vote was passed through the rank-and-file membership — which has nearly tripled in size over the past year since the election of Green Party Leader Zack Polanski and left-wing voters leaving the Labour Party over its stance on Gaza. But Polanski himself did not vote on the motion, and other Green Party leaders distanced themselves from the motion.

Backlash has also emerged within the U.K., including from members of the Labour Party — some of whom are calling on Labour leader Andy Burnham to rule out forming a coalition with the Greens.

This is not surprising, Charlie Hore, a socialist activist in the U.K., explained to Truthout — but it ignores the fact that the Palestine solidarity movement has transformed U.K. politics.

“At the Labour Party conference earlier this month, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband was forced to say that the Labour government had gotten Gaza wrong. What forced that is the massive shift in public opinion in the last couple of years in favor of Palestine and against Israel,” explained Hore.

The solidarity movement, and widespread shift in opinion, has also been credited as key to the Labour government imposing sanctions on Israeli settlements last month.

“Every major party in British politics supports the state of Israel, despite the occasional criticism,” Hore said. “The Greens have chosen the side of Palestine, and that’s going to be a good thing for taking the Palestine solidarity movement forward.”

We now have three full months of data since Google changed its search to feature AI results. The numbers are worse than we anticipated. Overall readership that comes to Truthout through Google is down 54 percent against last year. The number of new readers who discover Truthout via Google searches is down 49 percent, and returning users from Google are down 51 percent.

We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We anticipate a loss of roughly $500,000 in online revenue as a result of this massive traffic plunge in the next year alone.

The only way we can keep publishing is with strong reader support. We are asking you to start a monthly donation to Truthout today — anything you can do, whether $5 or $25, makes a difference.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Quebec election day goes smoothly in Nunavik, officials say
content:
Officials say voting in the Ungava riding during Quebec’s provincial election is unfolding with no issues — a stark contrast from the 2025 federal election.


Polling stations are open in every community in the region, with two elections officers in each community, said Élections Québec spokesperson Julie St-Arnaud-Drolet in an email on Monday.


From Sept. 26 to Sept. 30, the advance polling dates in Nunavik, election staff helped residents get on the electors list to participate in the election, she said.


Election staff also recruited and trained locals to run the election, she added.


“In most communities, they were able to hire local residents; as a result, voters have access to services in Inuktitut today, on election day,” she said.


Kuujjuaq deputy Mayor Claude Gadbois said the voting process was smooth in his community.


“Everything seems to be under control,” Gadbois told Nunatsiaq News over Facebook on Monday afternoon.


During the 2025 federal election, some

Nunavimmiut were unable to cast ballots

. On election day in April, polling stations in two communities did not open at all, while seven others had reduced hours.


Elections Canada released a report last November that said a lack of planning and almost no local outreach were responsible for the problems.


The polls for the 2026 provincial election close at 8 p.m. Monday. Five candidates are

running

 in Ungava, Quebec’s largest riding by geography.


Voters can cast their ballot from their village’s municipal office, except for those in Kuujjuaraapik, who must go to the community’s cultural centre.

author: Taina Da Silva
title: Near Grassy Narrows, an Elder shows us how using the land also protects it
content:
Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich’s Land Back Garden on the outskirts of the Grassy Narrows First Nation. Photo by Taina Da Silva


I’m thinking about the power of my treaty rights as I drive to meet with Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich — Roberta Keesick — on a late summer day on the outskirts of Grassy Narrows.


Gwawich is an activist and trapper who has substantial experience of being on the land and creating land-based learning systems for our community. She grew up in our territory with a traditional Anishinaabek family, and she works to restore our traditional ways. 


As I pull into the site, Gwawich offers me some ripe vegetables — a squash, green beans and tomatoes — that she’s harvested from an extensive garden nearby. 


Gwawich and I are ten minutes outside of the reserve line of Grassy Narrows First Nation, a small and semi-remote community in northwestern Ontario. We sit at an off-grid campsite and community garden which Gwawich started by herself to host her Seven Grandfathers Teachings Program.


The Seven Grandfather Teachings — love, respect, bravery, truth, honesty, humility, and wisdom — are what Gwawich’s social program follows, and she hopes her program will impact Grassy in a way that will bring us Anishinaabek back to the land and culture. 


“Colonization has changed our ways of thinking,” she says. 


A lake in the traditional homelands of Grassy Narrows First Nation. Photo by Taina Da Silva


As the lake glistens in the background, Gwawich talks about how she is determined to decolonize our community from decades of learned behaviour — stemming from the reserve system that relocated people in our community, to the residential “school” system and

devastating mercury pollution

, which have all been an upheaval to our traditional ways.


Her campsite is available for any band members who want to get away from the reserve, and the garden is another free resource where members are often invited to pick fresh food.


“Land Back Garden” is painted on a wooden sign and it sits front-and-centre of the garden. Another sign near the campsite greets visitors to the “Seven Grandfather Teachings Program — Land Based Family Healing Initiative.”

This program is how families from Grassy are now able to access different opportunities designed to bring land based learning to the community, and it is what our aboriginal land title permits us to do in our territories. 


Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich’s program is helping Grassy Narrows members return to their traditional ways. Photo by Taina Da Silva


What started as a community-wide gardening initiative in 2020 has grown into the off-grid garden and campsite, a monthly food program in the community, and a small sewing building right in the reserve — all operating through outside funding.


Children from the reserve are able to experience what it might have been like for the older generations to gather traditionally, share food, and play games like the old days — and with some contemporary additions.


Today, there are community events with bungee trampolines, rock climbing, horse rides and even a zipline, Gwawich tells me with true pride. 


Gwawich speaks excitedly about a farmers’ market coming up, where she will be taking vegetables from the Land Back Garden to give away to Grassy families. 


She reminds me that “being out on the land makes our rights stronger,” and that running the site is a way to protect the land — and our rights under Treaty 3.


This is an area of land which I mistakenly used to associate as a settler hunting camp on so-called “Crown land,” before I learned about traditional land use areas and our history of ancient rock paintings, burial grounds and artifacts found across our territory. 


It takes community members like Gwawich to figure out ways to navigate the colonial systems that have been imposed on us, and decolonize our ways of thinking.


Gwawich remembers a time when the entirety of Grassy Narrows spoke our language and lived off trapping and fishing incomes when she was a child in the 1960s and 70s. 


“Even my siblings were helping with trapping and fishing when they were nine and ten years old,” she said, and we laughed at the idea of that happening now — because that is a lost tradition for Anishinaabek families.


Residential “schools” — an intentional violation of our human rights — and the resulting language and culture loss are not easily forgotten about in our communities. Repairing the losses and devastation is not a simple …

author: Chad Nelson
title: နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေရဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေအပေါ် တိုက်ခိုက်မှုဟာ တကယ်တော့ အာရုံလွှဲတာပါပဲ
content:
Chad Nelson

.

The Political Class’s War on Immigrants is a Diversion

, January 30, 2015. Translated into Burmese by Hein Htet Kyaw.


ဂျန်နဝါရီ ၂၈ ရက်နေ့မှာ လော်ရက်တာ လင်းချ် (Loretta Lynch) ကို အစိုးရရှေ့နေချုပ် အဖြစ် ခန့်အပ်ဖို့ အမေရိကန် ဆီးနက်စစ်ဆေးမေးမြန်းခြင်း စတင်ချိန်မှာ၊ ရီပတ်ဘလစ်ကန်တွေဟာ အစိုးရက “တရားမဝင် ခိုးဝင်သူတွေ” လို့ သတ်မှတ်ထားတဲ့ လူတန်းစားအပေါ် သူမ ဘယ်လောက်အထိ အလိုက်သင့် ပေါင်းသင်းမလဲဆိုတာ မေးဖို့ အရမ်းစိတ်အားထက်သန်နေကြတာပါ။ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေအပေါ် တင်းကြပ်တဲ့ ဂျက်ဖ် ဆက်ရှင်နိစ် (Jeff Sessions – R-AL) နဲ့ အပြန်အလှန် မေးမြန်းမှုတစ်ခုမှာ၊ ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်က အမေရိကမှာ အလုပ်လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့် ဘယ်သူ့မှာ ရှိလဲဆိုတာ လင်းချ် ဘယ်လိုယုံကြည်လဲ မေးခဲ့ပါတယ်။ သီးသန့်အနေနဲ့ပြောရရင်၊ “ဘယ်သူက ပိုပြီး လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့်ရှိသလဲ – တရားဝင်လာတဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူလား၊ နိုင်ငံသားလား၊ ဒါမှမဟုတ် တိုင်းပြည်ထဲ တရားမဝင် ဝင်လာတဲ့သူလား” လို့ သူက မေးခဲ့တာပါ။ လင်းချ်ကတော့ ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်ရဲ့ မေးခွန်းအတုအယောင်ကို လိမ္မာပါးနပ်စွာ ရှောင်လွှဲခဲ့ပြီး၊ လူတစ်ယောက်ဟာ ဒီမှာ တရားမဝင် ရှိနေရင်တောင် အမေရိကရဲ့ လုပ်သားအင်အားထဲမှာ ပါဝင်သူတစ်ယောက်အနေနဲ့ ရှိနေတာကိုပဲ ပိုသဘောကျတယ်လို့ ပြန်ဖြေခဲ့ပါတယ်။


ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်ရဲ့ မေးခွန်းထုတ်ပုံနည်းလမ်းနဲ့ သူလိုချင်နေတဲ့ အဖြေ ဟာ နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေရဲ့ လိမ်ညီနေတဲ့ အတွေးအခေါ်ကို အများကြီး ဖော်ပြနေပါတယ်။ ဝါရှင်တန်က နှစ်ပါတီစလုံးမှာပါတဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေကို တိုက်ခိုက်တဲ့အုပ်စုက ရှယ်လ်ဒွန် ရစ်ချ်မန်း (Sheldon Richman) မှတ်ချက်ပြုသလိုပဲ “အလုပ်လုပ်ခွင့် ပေးပိုင်ခွင့်ဆိုတာ သူတို့ပေးမှ ရတာ” လို့ ယုံကြည်ထားကြတာပါ။ ဝမ်းနည်းစရာက အဲဒီယုံကြည်ချက်ဟာ ဒီတိုင်းပြည်ရဲ့ ဥပဒေဖြစ်နေတာပါပဲ။ ဒီနေ့ခေတ်မှာ ဘယ်သူအလုပ်လုပ်ခွင့်ရှိလဲဆိုတဲ့ မေးခွန်းကို ဝါရှင်တန်က ဗျူရိုကရက်တွေနဲ့ သူတို့ဆီကနေ လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့် လက်ဝါးကြီးအုပ်ခွင့် လာဝယ်နေတဲ့ အကျိုးစီးပွားကာကွယ်ရေး အုပ်စုတွေကပဲ အဓိက ဆုံးဖြတ်နေကြတာပါ။ မင်းအနေနဲ့ ကိုယ်ကြိုက်တဲ့ အလုပ်ကို လွတ်လပ်စွာ လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့်ရှိတယ်လို့ ထင်ချင်ထင်နေလိမ့်မယ်၊ ဒါပေမဲ့ အစိုးရက စည်းကမ်းချက်တွေ အမျိုးမျိုး ထုတ်ပြန်ပြီး မင်းရဲ့ ရွေးချယ်ခွင့်တွေကို အများကြီး ကျဉ်းမြောင်းအောင် လုပ်ပစ်လိုက်တာပါ။ အဲဒီအတားအဆီးတွေကို ကျော်လွှားနိုင်ခဲ့ရင်တောင် အစိုးရ သတ်မှတ်ထားတဲ့ စည်းမျဉ်းစည်းကမ်း နွံထဲမှာ ရုန်းကန်နေရတာနဲ့တင် မင်းရဲ့ ကျွမ်းကျင်မှုကို အပြည့်အဝ ထုတ်မသုံးနိုင်တော့ဘဲ ဖြစ်နေရပါတယ်။


နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေဟာ သူတို့ရဲ့ ပြည်သူတွေအပေါ် လွှမ်းမိုးချုပ်ကိုင်ထားနိုင်ဖို့ ဒီလိုမျိုး အရမ်းအရေးပါတဲ့ လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့်ကို မှီခိုနေကြတာပါ။ ပြည်သူတွေကို အလုပ်လုပ်ခွင့် ပေးပိုင်ခွင့်ရှိနေတာ၊ နဲ့ အဲဒီခွင့်ပြုချက်နဲ့အတူ ပါလာတဲ့ စည်းကမ်းသတ်မှတ်ချက်တွေ အားလုံးက ကပ်ပါး နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေကို သူတို့အိတ်ကပ်ထဲ အထိရောက်ဆုံး နည်းလမ်းနဲ့ ပိုက်ဆံထည့်နိုင်အောင် ကူညီပေးထားပါတယ်။ အလုပ်တစ်ခုဟာ တရားမဝင် ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူရဲ့ အလုပ်ဖြစ်ဖြစ်၊ အမေရိကန် မှောင်ခိုဈေးကွက်က အလုပ်သမားရဲ့ အလုပ်ဖြစ်ဖြစ် စည်းမျဉ်းမရှိတဲ့ ဈေးကွက်တွေဆီ လမ်းကြောင်းပြောင်းသွားရင် နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေအနေနဲ့ အဲဒါကို စောင့်ကြည့်ဖို့နဲ့ ဆက်ကြေးတောင်းဖို့ ခက်သွားပါတယ်။ သူတို့ရဲ့ ရှုပ်ထွေးလှတဲ့ အခွန်၊ လုပ်အား၊ နဲ့ အုပ်ချုပ်ရေး ဥပဒေတွေကို မလိုက်နာရင်၊ သက်ဆိုင်ရာ အသက်မွေးဝမ်းကျောင်း လုပ်ငန်းတစ်ခုလုံးပေါ်မှာ လိုင်စင်စနစ်တွေ အထပ်ထပ် တင်ထားတာကို မလိုက်နာရင် မင်းရဲ့ အသက်မွေးဝမ်းကျောင်းလုပ်ငန်းပါ ရုတ်တရက် ဖျက်ဆီးခံရနိုင်ခြေ ရှိပါတယ်။ ဒီစနစ်တစ်ခုလုံးကို ထုတ်လုပ်သူတွေနဲ့ စားသုံးသူတွေကို ကာကွယ်ပေးနေပါတယ်ဆိုပြီး အတုအယောင် လိမ်ညာရောင်းချထားတာပါ။


တရားမဝင် ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချမှု သက်သက်က ဗျူရိုကရက်တွေကို ခြိမ်းခြောက်နေတာ မဟုတ်ပါဘူး။ သူတို့ အမှန်တကယ် ကြောက်တာက ထိန်းချုပ်မထားတဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းလုပ်သားတွေဆီကရတဲ့ ဝင်ငွေလမ်းကြောင်းတွေကို ချုပ်ကိုင်ခွင့် ဆုံးရှုံးသွားမှာကိုပါ။ ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်နဲ့ ကွန်ဂရက်ထဲက သူ့လို နယ်စပ်စောင့် စိစစ်ရေးသမားတွေဟာ သူတို့ကြောက်ရွံ့မှုကို “ငါတို့ နဲ့ သူတို့” ဆိုတဲ့ စကားလုံးတွေနဲ့ ဖုံးကွယ်ပြီး ရေးကြီးခွင်ကျယ် စကားလုံးအလှတွေ သုံးနေကြတာပါ၊ ဒါဟာ အရေးပါတဲ့ နိုင်ငံရေး ရည်ရွယ်ချက်အတွက် ပြုလုပ်ထားတဲ့ ပြဇာတ်တစ်ခုပါပဲ။ ဒီလို လှည့်ကွက်မျိုးနဲ့ နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေက မင်းတို့ကို လှည့်စားထားတာပါ။ သူတို့ ကြောက်နေတာဟာ အခွန်ဘဏ္ဍာ ဆုံးရှုံးမှာကို မဟုတ်ဘဲ၊ “မင်းတို့ရဲ့” အလုပ်တွေ၊ “မင်းတို့ရဲ့” ကျန်းမာရေးစောင့်ရှောက်ခွင့်တွေ၊ နဲ့ “မင်းတို့ရဲ့” လူမှုဖူလုံရေးတွေ ဆုံးရှုံးမှာကို ကြောက်နေရတာပါဆိုပြီး ယုံအောင် လှည့်စားထားတာပါ။ တရားဝင် ရှိနေပြီး အလုပ်လုပ်နေသူတွေ (အခွန်ဆောင်နေသူတွေ) ကိုတော့ မျိုးချစ်စိတ်ရှိသူတွေအဖြစ် သတ်မှတ်ပေးထားပါတယ်။ အစိုးရက သူတို့ရဲ့ လစာထဲက ဖြတ်တောက်ယူနေတာကို မုန်းတီးစရာလို့ မမြင်ဘဲ အားလုံးရဲ့ ကောင်းဖက်အတွက် အရေးပါတဲ့ ပါဝင်ဆောင်ရွက်မှုအဖြစ် ကြိုဆိုကြရပါတယ်။ ခွင့်ပြုချက်မရှိဘဲ အလုပ်လုပ်သူတွေကိုတော့ ရန်သူတွေ၊ တရားဝင် အလုပ်လုပ်နေသူတွေရဲ့ မွန်မြတ်တဲ့ အလုပ်ကို ဖျက်ဆီးနေသူတွေအဖြစ် ပုံဖော်ကြပါတယ်။ “မင်းတို့” က လူကောင်း၊ “သူတို့” က လူဆိုး ပေါ့။ နိုင်ငံရေးအရ အင်အားမရှိတဲ့ တရားမဝင် ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေဟာ ဝါရှင်တန်အတွက် တိုက်ခိုက်ရ အလွယ်ဆုံး ပစ်မှတ်ဖြစ်နေပြီး နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေရဲ့ စိတ်ကူးယဉ် ပြဿနာရှာမှုတွေအတွက် လွယ်လွယ်ကူကူ …

title: Event Announcement: Resisting ICE – Strategies from Minneapolis, Chicago, and Durham
content:
Event Description:

 One year after Midway Blitz,

social movements across Chicago continue to fight deportations and detention.


At this panel discussion you’ll hear from people organizing against ICE in cities around the country, including

a member of the #Minnesota15,

 as well as organizers from Chicago and Durham, NC.


Bring a friend, coworker, or neighbor! Social at a nearby bar to follow panel discussion.


When:

 Friday, October 9th | 6:30 – 8:00 PM


Where

: Pilsen Community Books – 1531 W. 18th St., Chicago, IL. 60608


La discusión se llevará a cabo en inglés con interpretación al español.

author: Duaa e Zahra Shah
title: Iran’s teachers movement perseveres against all odds
content:
This article

Iran’s teachers movement perseveres against all odds

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Sunlight filtered through the trees separating the headquarters of the Plan and Budget Organization in Tehran as

300 teachers

 gathered outside to protest on Sept. 6. Their demands were simple: salaries that keep pace with inflation, fair pay scales and improved health and welfare services.


They knew they were taking an enormous risk. 


For years, educators across Iran have

taken to the streets

 to demand fair wages, better working conditions, the release of detained teachers, the constitutionally guaranteed rights to free education for all children and to peaceful assembly and association. For years,

they have faced

 arrests, enforced disappearances, prosecutions on national security charges, dismissals, imprisonment and solitary confinement. 


Teachers and teachers’ union activists played a prominent role in the

January 2026

 uprising, when people across the country called for freedom and an end to the Islamic Republic system of government. In response, they were heavily targeted. By July, at least

60

had been arrested

, prosecuted or imprisoned. At least

14 have been killed

. Still, against all odds, Iranian teachers have kept their movement alive.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


The Iranian teachers’ movement is not organized through a single union. Local and provincial teachers’ associations operate across the country, while an umbrella network called the

Coordinating Council of Iranian Teachers’ Trade Associations

, or CCITTA, links many of them. The structure allows teachers to organize locally while coordinating actions across the country.


Some of these actions, like protests and public statements, are impossible to miss. Others are less confrontational and more relational: debating movement priorities, supporting imprisoned colleagues and their families, building solidarity with other social movements, or simply getting together to hike or read or watch a film. Together, they knit together a movement that has proven resilient against virtually every form of repression, from internet shutdowns to detentions and killings, while continuing to press its demands.


‘A continuation of my responsibility as a teacher’


Mohammad Habibi became a teacher in 2003. For him, it was never just a job; it felt like a social responsibility. But he soon realized that quality education for students could not be fully achieved without protecting teachers’ rights. So he joined the Iranian Teachers’ Trade Association and later took on several roles within the CCITTA. He is currently its spokesperson. 


“My trade union activism wasn’t separate from teaching,” he said. “I saw it as a continuation of my responsibility as a teacher. Teachers have a duty that goes beyond teaching textbooks. They must defend the right to education, student dignity, educational justice and freedom of thought.”


Like Habibi, the nine teachers interviewed for this story described demands that encompass both their own rights and those of their students. They want salaries and pensions that reflect the real cost of living, job security, meaningful participation in education policy, freedom of expression and association, and the release of their imprisoned colleagues.


But they’re also calling for free, high-quality and equitable public education for all children, regardless of ethnicity or gender, while opposing the privatization and commercialization of education.


For Esmaeil Abdi, the former general secretary of the Tehran Teachers’ Trade Association, who spent nearly nine years in prison for his activism, the fight against privatization is inseparable from the fight for equality. “If education becomes a commodity whose quality depends on a family’s economic ability, social inequality is reproduced from one generation to the next,” he said.


Teachers also advocate for every child’s right to receive education in their mother tongue alongside Persian, arguing that Iran’s linguistic and cultural diversity should be reflected in its schools.


Over the years, the movement has won concessions on some of these demands, like pension increases, the implementation of the Teacher Ranking Law (specifying pay tiers) and corresponding salary increases, and a voice in the management of their retirement fund. author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Afghan Women Are Restricted, But They Cannot Be Silenced. They Continue to Be Agents of Change in Afghanistan.
content:
Afghan women have been living under one of the most repressive systems in the world, as the Taliban continue to impose restrictive edicts – over 160 in total to date. These orders restrict their ability to work, attend school, move freely and even leave their homes without a male guardian. Yet despite the barriers the Taliban have imposed, Afghan women continue to be at the forefront of efforts to build peace and stability in Afghanistan.

Peace and security extends beyond just political conversations. They also include the “daily strategies Afghan women employ to defend human rights and generate conditions for peace.” According to a report by the Georgetown Institute for Women, Peace, and Security, 81% of Afghan women participate in efforts focused on women’s and girl’s education, 64% in economic empowerment, and another 54% in health & reproductive rights and services. Afghan women are also engaged in health and reproductive rights and services, by roughly 9%, compared to women from other regions of South Asia.

These figures demonstrate the perseverance, leadership, and problem solving of Afghan women. Afghanistan is facing a reproductive health crisis, with maternal mortality rapidly increasing since the Taliban took over in 2021. The loss of international funding and organizational support has also greatly affected the reproductive health programs. To help fill these gaps and address the mounting health issues facing women and girls, Afghan women have stepped in to provide critical support and services.

This sense of responsibility extends beyond just responding to immediate needs; it reflects the determination of Afghan women to protect and strengthen their communities despite the restrictions imposed on them. While many formal opportunities for education, employment, and political participation have been taken away after 2021, women have continued to find ways to serve their communities. For example, they have established online schools, supported women’s access to healthcare services, organized community-based initiatives, and advocated for women’s rights.

The significant role women continue to play in activities that promote peace and security demonstrate that resilience is not just their ability to endure oppression. It is also the ability to adapt, organize, and create solutions especially in an environment that has been designed to limit their every move and every opportunity.

Their resilience is particularly significant because many of these efforts occur in an environment where women are already facing risks to their lives. Their actions demonstrate their collective responsibility, where women have repeatedly stepped forward to address unmet needs themselves.

Their resilience also challenges the perception of Afghan women in the media solely as victims of the Taliban restrictions imposed on them. While challenges of these restrictions are severe, Afghan women have found ways to find space and operate within them. They are evidence that resilience can take many forms.

Their efforts demonstrate that, even under deeply restrictive circumstances, Afghan women continue to shape the social fabric of their communities and contribute to building a more stable and peaceful Afghanistan. This is also evident in how Afghan women see and define themselves. Among women working in the peace and security field, 65% of women describe themselves as activists while 37% of them describe themselves as human rights defenders. As one activist explained, “As an activist woman, I am not a victim of war, but an architect of social peace, and this is a voice that must be heard globally.”

Their work in education, healthcare, economic empowerment, and community development demonstrates that Afghan women are not simply recipients of aid or victims of conflict, they are powerful agents of change. Their persistence and leadership are an important source of strength for their communities and a reminder that peacebuilding in Afghanistan cannot succeed without the full participation of Afghan women at the table.

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Activists Are Pushing Cities and Companies to Cancel Parking Contracts With ICE
content:
The Trump administration’s abduction and deportation machine is multifaceted. There are clear-cut components — agents, shackles, and jails — and less obvious, although no less essential, ones — cars and parking spaces.


In an effort to impede the attacks on immigrants, mayors of some of the country’s largest cities, including

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani

,

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson

, and

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu

, have issued executive orders

banning Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

 from using city-owned parking lots and properties.


But even in cities where mayors have banned ICE from using government-owned properties, ICE still has free reign to contract with private companies. After the federal agency

posted a notice

 seeking “Surge Parking” in 14 cities, including Boston, Wu

released a public letter

 to

local parking garage and lot owners

, warning them that if ICE were “to procure such resources, it would constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation, creating potentially significant risks to public safety and halting economic activity across our entire region.”


“Today, I ask you to join us: Reject any proposition by ICE to facilitate an attack on the people of Boston,”

she wrote

. “In the face of escalating attacks on cities across the country, we have repeatedly seen that the strongest defense is solidarity.”


In the Boston suburb of Burlington, Massachusetts, Bearing Witness New England has been holding weekly protests outside ICE’s Boston Field Office, where people are

held for days

 in inhumane conditions. Activists say ICE has been keeping its vehicles in a nearby parking lot owned by local developer National Development.


According to a report by

NPR

 affiliate

WBUR

, the company sent a letter to local activists in February, stating that ICE vehicles were being “improperly parked” in its parking spaces, and that it had “reached an arrangement with ICE that they would no longer park their vehicles on our property.”


However, the company also said that the government agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), has

rights to use the garage

 and the company does not have authority over how the FAA parcels out parking spaces to other federal agencies, according to

WBUR

’s report.


Nathan Phillips, a Boston University professor who organizes with the Burlington-area coalition

Building Up Resilience Networks (B.U.R.N.)

, says ICE has continued to park in sections of lots National Development leases to the FAA that exceed what the lease allows.


Protests that target parking garages are “throwing sand in the gears” of ICE’s deportation and abduction machine, he says.


“So much of their operation depends on logistics of transport and travel,” Phillips told

Truthout

. “It’s human trafficking, and so if we can go after the trafficking, the means by which they’re doing this, that can have a really effective impact.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


Fellow B.U.R.N. activist Josh Model says National Development’s recent actions contradict its public image as a

philanthropic company

 committed to improving communities.


“National Development Corporation, which, as a local developer, likes to promote that they’re cognizant of community needs and give to charity and all these nice things,” but they’re “letting ICE stage kidnappings” from their property, said Model.


While the government spending website,

usaspending.gov

, only lists 12 active contracts for parking spaces, as of September 28, the true number of parking lots that ICE uses is likely much higher, said Model. It’s difficult to untangle where ICE is parking, in part, because many of the contracts are not with ICE, but through another federal agency, the

General Services Administration

 (GSA), he said. The GSA manages government buildings and real estate, and owns or leases space in more than 8,300 buildings, according to an

explainer

 on the agency published by the Congressional Research Service.


In the case of National Development, ICE is using parking leased by the GSA for the FAA, according to Model.


Of the 12 contracts found on usaspending.gov, two were with the Philadelphia Parking Authority (PPA). The

PPA website

 states that, among other responsibilities, it coordinates “the efforts of public agencies concerning parking” and establishes and operates public …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Lili Reinhart Wants To Adapt a Lesbian Vampire Novella — Let Her!
content:
feature image photo by Emma McIntyre / Staff via Getty Images

Bisexual baddie Lili Reinhart has been on a press tour for her new film, The Love Hypothesis, and I’ve been really enjoying her interviews. The film seems to be the CLASSIC fake dating trope come to life — in fact, the book it’s based on started as Star Wars fanfic! — and despite the movie being seemingly extremely heterosexual, on this tour, she has been quick to remind interviewers and fans that she’s queer. She has also said she hopes in her next project is gay. (Fingers crossed!)

In one video interview she says, “I’m instantly way more interested in doing a movie if my character is a little gay,” she continued. “Because I’m a little gay.” She also reads a comment about being one of “the five pillars of bisexuality with preference to women” and she called it an honor.

In that same interview, she also mentioned that she’s trying to get a film adaptation of a lesbian vampire novella made but that Hollywood seems “too afraid” to make it. She also wonders aloud who WOULDN’T want to make it, a sentiment I agree with. The general assumption people have been making is that it would be an adaptation of the 1872 novella Carmilla, which the popular webseries starring Natasha Negovanlis and Elise Bauman was based on, and I think that would be fun if true. I personally think there can’t be too many adaptations of that novella. The gayer the better. In fact, I just read Hungerstone by Kat Dunn, which is one of a few retellings of that novella and offers a very different take than the webseries.

I, for one, am delighted that Lili keeps making her press tour about a heterosexual love story as queer as she can, and I’m glad she’s using it to pitch her idea. I really hope someone with the means is paying attention and can pick it up and let her run with it.

In my opinion, there’s no such thing as too many lesbian vampire adaptations in general. When is someone going to make a Bury Our Bones in the Midnight Soil miniseries? A movie version of A Long Time Dead, anyone? Let’s get all the lesbian vampires out here while we’re at it. Tis the season!

You can watch the full video interview here.

author: Bruno Fonseca
title: Como o agro e o interior podem explicar diminuição de votos para Lula
content:
O domingo do primeiro turno terminou com uma surpresa, ao menos para quem acompanhava a maioria das pesquisas eleitorais e também para os próprios candidatos. “Confesso que estava convencido de que iria ganhar no primeiro turno”,

disse

 Lula ontem. O atual presidente marcou 3,3 milhões de votos a menos do que no primeiro turno de 2022, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro conseguiu 5 milhões de votos a mais que seu pai, Jair.


O resultado pode ser explicado por vários fatores: como a

Agência Pública


mostrou

,

escândalos políticos podem ter favorecido o desejo “antissistema” que – apesar de ser uma grande contradição –, é usado politicamente por Flávio e bolsonaristas.

 O caso do Master, inclusive, não foi capaz de impedir que muitos políticos diretamente citados nas investigações e vazamentos ligados ao banco

conseguissem

 se reeleger. Isso inclui o próprio Flávio, investigado por suspeitas de lavagem de dinheiro, corrupção e evasão de divisas em relação ao financiamento do filme Dark Horse, sobre seu pai. Flávio pediu dinheiro diretamente para Daniel Vorcaro, trocou dezenas de mensagens com o ex-banqueiro e marcou encontros com ele.


Além dos escândalos políticos, outras variáveis ajudam a entender a diminuição de votos de Lula e o crescimento de Flávio, e elas ficam evidentes no próprio mapa do Brasil. Levantamento de dados feito pelo cientista político Marco Antonio Faganello, pesquisador do Centro de Política e Economia do Setor Público da Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV/CEPESP), mostra que

Lula perdeu mais votos em municípios que não são capitais, e essa perda é ainda mais gritante em cidades menores onde a participação do agro na economia é grande.

 “Onde o agro está em mais de 50% no PIB, no conjunto, Lula perdeu 8% dos votos em relação a 2022”, aponta.


A análise de Faganello mostra que municípios pequenos do interior, com alto PIB per capita, proporção de moradores que se declaram brancos e jovens mais alta e com grande atividade agropecuária estão onde Lula mais perdeu votos proporcionalmente a 2022. É esse o tipo de perfil de vários municípios de Goiás, estado onde a diminuição dos votos para Lula foi a mais significativa na proporção com 2022.


O pesquisador também aponta que o Nordeste, apesar de ser um reduto tradicional de Lula e não ter registrado uma queda significativa nos votos para o atual presidente, foi onde Flávio mais avançou. “A direita cresceu nos nove estados do Nordeste. Flávio superou o resultado de Bolsonaro em 98% dos 1.794 municípios da região. No Nordeste, Lula perdeu poucos votos, mas a direita cresceu em todos os estados: de 27% para 30,9% dos votos válidos”, detalha.


Na entrevista, Faganello também avalia como a abstenção, apesar de ter sido recorde, não parece ter impactado a perda de votos de Lula no Brasil como um todo, com exceção de Salvador, onde a

ausência de eleitores

 impactou a votação do petista. Além disso, para o pesquisador, a proporção de evangélicos entre a população pode não explicar essa mudança. Contudo, Faganello ressalta que ainda há dados que o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral deve divulgar que podem detalhar esses aspectos.


Confira os principais trechos da entrevista aqui.


Marco Antonio Faganello é cientista político e pesquisador do Centro de Política e Economia do Setor Público da Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV/CEPESP)


Na sua análise, você conclui que Lula teve menos votos em 2026 em relação ao primeiro turno de 2022 em 98% dos municípios do Brasil. Mas isso aconteceu diferente nas cidades pequenas e nas capitais e também a partir de outros fatores, como atividade agropecuária. Você pode explicar melhor essa diferença?


Estamos falando em votação proporcional, isto é, no quanto os votos que foram para o Lula em 2022 aumentaram ou diminuíram em 2026, proporcionalmente.

Os dados mostram que essa queda foi maior sobretudo nos pequenos municípios e nos municípios ligados ao agro, além de ter um recorte por região do país. São esses os três principais fatores: tamanho, agro e região.


Sobre o tamanho dos municípios, quanto menor, mais Lula perdeu votos em relação a 2022. Nos municípios com até 5 mil habitantes, ele perde cerca de 7% [comparando 2026 a 2022]. Nos com mais de 500 mil habitantes, ele perde só 1%.


É importante ressaltar que isso é uma faceta, porque se você olha pra outro lado, em números absolutos, esse contingente de municípios pequenos não contribui tanto para a diminuição dos votos do Lula.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Dos policías bonaerenses a juicio por apremios ilegales contra un joven
content:
La Cámara de Apelación y Garantías en lo Penal de Azul confirmó la elevación a juicio de la causa que tiene como imputados a los policías bonaerenses Brian Nahuel Ríos y Agustín Villarreal, por la violenta y desproporcionada intervención que desencadenó la muerte de Nahuel Tasori, ocurrida en julio de 2023 en la ciudad de Tandil. Los policías llegan imputados por el delito de apremios ilegales, por haber golpeado y rociado con gas pimienta a la víctima cuando ya estaba reducida y esposada. A pesar del evidente estado de excitación por el consumo de estupefacientes, Tasori fue trasladado a la comisaría donde estuvo alojado durante varias horas hasta que lo llevaron al hospital donde finalmente murió. La Comisión Provincial por la Memoria (CPM), en su carácter de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura, participa en la causa como particular damnificado institucional (PDI).


El fallo de la Cámara de Apelación y Garantías en lo Penal de Azul –integrada por los magistrados Damián Pedro Cini, Carlos Paulino Pagliere y Gustavo Agustín Echevarría- llega como respuesta al recurso de apelación interpuesto por la defensora particular Noelia Soledad Pereyra, para quien la elevación a juicio dictada el pasado 10 de junio por el juez de garantías de Tandil José Alberto Moragas es una resolución arbitraria, infundada y lesiva de las garantías constitucionales de defensa en juicio.


El hecho que se ventila en esta causa ocurrió durante la madrugada del 28 de julio de 2023, cuando una mujer (cuya identidad no se reveló) llamó al 911 denunciando que un ladrón había saltado un paredón de un domicilio particular en la intersección de las calles Pasaje y Segundo Sombras de Tandil.


El llamado dio origen al arribo de un patrullero de servicio en el que se trasladaban Villarreal y Ríos. Cuando llegaron al lugar el presunto ladrón ya había sido reducido en el piso por los propios vecinos, que se habían alarmado con los gritos y los ruidos esa madrugada. Luego de esposar al joven, mientras intentaban introducirlo en el móvil policial uno de los agentes le dio un fuerte golpe de puño y el otro le roció la cara con gas pimienta, sin ninguna circunstancia de peligro inminente que amerite el uso de la fuerza física o la violencia.


Al momento de la aprehensión, Nahuel estaba en un estado de alteración y excitación por el consumo de estupefacientes. Pese a que sus síntomas eran evidente, los funcionarios policiales no aplicaron los protocolos para la intervención en casos de salud mental y adicciones, que consistían en convocar a personal de la salud para su intervención. Por el contrario, lo trasladaron esposado a la comisaría donde quedó alojado durante varias horas. A medida que pasaba el tiempo, el estado de Nahuel fue empeorando y cuando decidieron llevarlo al hospital ya era demasiado tarde: falleció a poco de ingresar.


Desde el comienzo, la instrucción judicial -a cargo del fiscal José Calonje- se centró en el accionar violento de Villarreal y Ríos en el momento de la aprehensión, pero sin ahondar en la responsabilidad de cuidado que tenían sobre la víctima que estaba bajo su custodia. De hecho, tanto en la elevación a juicio solicitada por el juez Moragas como en el reciente fallo de la Cámara, la muerte de la víctima apenas aparece mencionada, a pesar que ocurrió en el contexto de la aprehensión y debió considerarse que, con la atención profesional y medicación adecuada, podría haberse evitado.


Para la CPM –que participa de la causa como particular damnificado institucional (PDI)- el caso reviste mayor gravedad aún si se considera que el joven aprehendido violentamente fue llevado a una comisaría que ni siquiera tenía calabozos y allí fue mantenido durante horas en lugar de trasladarlo directamente a un centro de salud mental, considerando el notorio estado de excitación psicomotriz en que se encontraba.


Sin atender a esta responsabilidad policial por las personas que están bajo su custodia, la defensa de los policías intentó incluso recurrir la elevación a juicio por la imputación de apremios ilegales. Entre los ejes del planteo para solicitar el sobreseimiento, se destacaban una errónea valoración de la prueba, las presuntas contradicciones que afectarían la credibilidad de la única testigo de la conducta agresiva y la falta de valoración de evidencias que favorecen la posición de los policías imputados, entre otros aspectos.


Sin embargo, por mayoría de votos, los jueces Echevarría y Cini rechazaron el planteo …

author: anred
title: Se suspendió el juicio por el Jujeñazo de 2023
content:
Lo resolvió la Corte Suprema de Jujuy. El debate debía comenzar el 26 de octubre. Sin embargo, la causa contra los 19 militantes sociales que participaron de la enorme movilización por mejoras salariales y en contra la reforma constitucional que impulsaba el entonces gobernador Gerardo Morales continúa abierta.

Por Red Eco Alternativo.


La decisión del máximo tribunal provincial se dio a conocer luego de que las defensas de los acusados informaran formalmente sobre la existencia de conversaciones avanzadas con la Fiscalía con el objetivo de alcanzar una solución alternativa y global al conflicto procesal.


En diálogo con El Submarino Radio (FM Conectar 91.5), la abogada Mariana Vargas confirmó la notificación del tribunal y expresó que la suspensión representa un avance clave: “El motivo es que informamos a la Corte que estábamos en conversaciones con la Fiscalía para una solución alternativa. Lo habíamos pedido con una queja ante la Corte y con muchos otros planteos (…). Es un gran alivio para las 19 personas, para sus familias y para toda la comunidad, porque en definitiva era un intento de disciplinamiento del conjunto del pueblo respecto de reclamos justos, como fue el Jujeñazo”, explicó la abogada Mariana Vargas al programa El Submarino Radio, que se emite por FM Conectar 91.5).


El juicio contemplaba acusaciones por atentado y resistencia a la autoridad, lesiones leves agravadas a personal policial y daños.


La suspensión deriva en la prescripción de los delitos de mayor carga penal dentro de la causa. Según señala la letrada, las figuras de atentado y resistencia a la autoridad y lesiones se encuentran al límite de su plazo legal de persecución. Al frenarse la apertura de las audiencias, ambas calificaciones quedan virtualmente extintas por prescripción: “Lo que podría estar en debate, que es el tema de la prescripción de los delitos, ahora ya no estaría en debate (…). Lo central es que hay una decisión, una voluntad política de que no se haga el juicio. Esa es la esencia de la cuestión. Es lo que estábamos buscando y es lo que logramos”, agregó la abogada a El Submarino Radio.


Compartimos además la entrevista realizada por el Colectivo Radio Pueblo a Miguel Ramos, de AJI20 – Biblioteca Niñxs Pájaros, quien contó cómo reciben esta decisión y qué significa para quienes siguen reclamando que se termine la persecución y se haga justicia:
